one_pager.big_idea: When two things change together (correlation), it does not prove that one causes the other (causation): a hidden third factor, or chance, may explain it, and graphs can be drawn to mislead.
goals: I can plot a scatter graph and describe the correlation it shows.
I can explain why a correlation does not prove causation, name a possible confounding variable, and fix a misleading graph.

flow.what: Retrieval on the back of the worksheet: reaction times 0.18, 0.15, 0.20, 0.19 s: mean (0.18 s), range (0.05 s, one number), and the three verdicts. Slides 1 to 2.
Winter graph: hot drink sales and colds both rise from October to January. 'Do hot drinks cause colds?' Vote Yes / No / Not sure and give a partner one reason; do not reveal the answer yet. Slide 3.

Positive, negative and no correlation with three mini scatter graphs (arm gestures: up, down, flat); correlation is not causation; winter as a confounding variable; three possible explanations plus chance. Slides 4 to 6.

Matching cards (4 min): pattern cards P1 to P7 to hidden-factor cards Q to W, P7 is the fair test trap; measure arm span and height (5 min), voluntary, codes not names, results on the board; plot the class scatter graph (7 min); 2 minutes slack. Sample data card for any group running late. Slides 7 to 9. If short: skip measuring and use the sample data, or cut matching to P1, P2, P4, P7.

Fix the graph (5 min): pairs answer the battery advert questions and redraw the chart from zero (Q looks 4 times taller, really 0.6 hours, about 6%); verdict: not enough evidence yet; exit ticket and logbook line (3 min). Slides 10 to 12.

one_pager.practical: Groups match 7 pattern cards to hidden-factor cards, then measure each other's height (back to the wall, book on head, sticky note) and arm span (sticky notes at the middle fingertips) to the nearest cm with a tape measure, write results on the board by code and plot the class scatter graph of arm span against height.
one_pager.assessment: Scatter graph (Core) on the worksheet and corrected bar chart on the Fix the graph sheet: collect the Fix the graph sheets to check who can explain a misleading axis. Exit ticket: confounding variable and correlation type (links to skills check question 10). Logbook line under New words: correlation, causation, confounding variable, with one example of each.
hazards: Tape measures can snap back and cut fingers or hit faces: retract slowly and keep the metal end away from faces.
Measuring bodies can feel personal: measuring is voluntary, codes not names on the board, and no comments about anyone's size.
Students who prefer not to be measured take the Measurer or Recorder role; their row uses the sample data.
one_pager.language_note: Frames: 'As ___ increases, ___ increases / decreases.' 'This could also be explained by ___.' 'A correlation does not prove ___ because ___.' 'The graph is misleading because ___.' Chinese talk is welcome while matching cards and discussing the graph; measurements are called out in English ('one hundred and sixty-five centimetres'). Traps: 'correlation' and 'cause' are often used as if they mean the same thing; link 'confounding' to 'confusing the picture'; the plural of 'axis' is 'axes'.
watch_out: 'If two things rise together, one must cause the other', or 'a strong correlation proves causation': even strong correlations can come from a third factor.
'A bar chart that looks very different means a big difference': always check where the axis starts.
'One odd point ruins the pattern': an anomaly should be checked, not ignored or allowed to decide the verdict.
Measuring overruns: hand the sample data card to any group running late; everyone in the class follows the same shoes rule (all on or all off).
one_pager.next_week_link: Next week: fair trials with a control group, blinding and a placebo; this lesson's 'change only one thing to show cause' is the bridge. Keep the photograph of the class data: a group choosing claim 9 ('your arm span equals your height') in Week 7 can use it as pilot data but should still collect their own. During this week, for Week 5: check 24 identical pens write; print, fold and shuffle pen cards (Code 41 and 52); word lists, recall sheets, checkpoint papers; brief the incoming teacher on the trial secret.
